summary: Benchmarking has traditionally used constant packet sizes, which show device capability but differ from real traffic. Tests with a mix of sizes (IMIX) are sometimes added. This informational document specifies a way, called the IMIX Genome, to describe variable packet size mixes so they can be reproduced.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6985 answers a small but practical problem in network testing. When a lab tests a router by sending it a mixture of small and large packets, the results are only meaningful if everyone knows the exact order and size of those packets. The RFC defines a short code for that sequence, in which one letter stands for one packet size, so a test report can name its packet mix exactly and another lab can repeat it.

questions: how to specify packet size mix for testing
what are the imix genome code letters
subtitle: A short written name that spells out the exact sequence of packet sizes used in a load test.

tldr.problem: Benchmarking has always used one fixed packet size at a time, which reveals what a device can do but not what it meets in a real network. Tests with a mixture of sizes are added, and results that simply say "IMIX" cannot be compared or repeated.
tldr.mechanism: The IMIX Genome is a one-line code in which each letter stands for a packet size, so the exact repeating sequence of sizes is written down. Rules for custom sizes and for long or pseudorandom sequences are given too.
tldr.outcome: The document gives a repeatable way to describe a test's packet sizes, so two labs running the same test can be sure they sent the same bytes in the same order.

facts.label: Genome codes
facts.value: a to j for the fixed sizes, z for the MTU

facts.label: Custom code letters
facts.value: A to Z, three lower-case letters per size

today: RFC 6985 is an Informational RFC published in July 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines a notation for recording the packet-size sequence used in a load test, and nothing in it obliges any implementation to change.

sections.title: Why Fixed Sizes Are Not Enough
sections.content:
Benchmarking methodologies have always relied on test conditions with constant packet sizes, with the goal of understanding what network device capability has been tested. Tests with the smallest size stress the header processing capacity, and tests with the largest size stress the overall bit-processing capacity. Sizes in between may determine the transition between those two capacities.

Streams of constant packet size differ significantly from the conditions met in operational deployment, so additional tests are sometimes conducted with a mixture of packet sizes. The set of sizes used is often called an Internet Mix, or IMIX. The mixture a device will encounter is highly variable and depends on many factors, so an IMIX suited to one device and deployment will not be appropriate for another. The mix may nevertheless be known, and the tester may be asked to augment the fixed-size tests. The RFC also notes that the architecture for IP Flow Information Export in RFC 5470 provides one way to gather packet-size information on private networks.

The proposal is a way to specify the exact repeating sequence of packet sizes from the usual set of fixed sizes, called the IMIX Genome. The name is meant to convey that the entire test packet-size sequence can be replicated if the information is known, much as the information needed for biological replication does. The memo takes the position that it cannot be proven for all circumstances that the sequence of packet sizes does not affect the test result, so a standardised specification of that sequence is valuable.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing with one packet size at a time tells you what a device can do. Testing with a realistic mixture tells you what it will actually meet. The trouble is that "a realistic mixture" is not the same in every lab, so the results cannot be compared.

sections.title: What This Covers and What It Does Not
sections.content:
The method defines how to specify unambiguously the sequence of packet sizes used in a load test, on the assumption that a relevant mix of sizes is known to the tester and that the length of the repeating sequence is not very long, in other words under 100 packets. The genome allows an exact sequence to be communicated as a single-line name, which resolves the current ambiguity in results that simply refer to IMIX.

The RFC is emphatic that this aspect matters. No ability has been demonstrated to extrapolate results from one IMIX to another, and certainly none to extrapolate results to other circumstances, even when the mix varies only slightly.

Two limits are set on the ambition. Documenting the exact sequence is ideal, but the memo also covers the case where the sequence of sizes is very long or may be generated by a pseudorandom process. And it is called a colossal non-goal to standardise one or more versions of the IMIX itself; that has been discussed many times on the benchmarking working group's mailing list. The goal is to enable customisation with minimal constraints while fostering repeatable testing once the fixed-size testing is complete. The requirements are written for those performing and reporting laboratory tests, in order to improve clarity and repeatability.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is for short repeating sequences of packet sizes. It does not try to say which mixture anyone should use, because that choice depends on the network being represented.

sections.title: The Genome Code
sections.content:
The IMIX Genome is written in the form IMIX - 123456...x, where each number is replaced by the letter that corresponds to the size of the packet at that position in the sequence. The letters cover the standard sizes of RFC 2544 and the larger jumbo sizes: a for 64 bytes, b for 128, c for 256, d for 512, e for 1024, f for 1280, g for 1518, h for 2112, i for 9000 and j for 16000, with z standing for the maximum transmission unit. A note warns that the four-octet Ethernet frame check sequence may fail to detect bit errors in the larger jumbo frames.

A five-packet sequence with sizes 64, 64, 64, 1280 and 1518 is therefore written IMIX - aaafg. If the letter z is used, the tester must specify the length of the maximum transmission unit in the report, since the code alone does not carry it.

The approach allows some flexibility but has constraints. Packet sizes not defined by RFC 2544 would have to be approximated by the sizes available in the table, and the genome for very long sequences can become undecipherable by people. The RFC also asks testers two questions they must answer and record: whether the sequence applies to each source and destination address pair, across multiple pairs in sets, or across all pairs; and whether it applies to each tester port, across multiple ports in sets, or across all ports. The chosen configuration is expressed as a table of source address and port or blade, destination address and port or blade, and the corresponding IMIX. A blade is a component in a multi-component device chassis.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter is one packet size. Writing the sequence out as letters tells the whole story in a few characters: aaafg means a 64-byte packet, another, another, then 1280 bytes and 1518 bytes, over and over.

sections.title: Custom Sizes
sections.content:
When the sizes needed are not in the standard table, a custom IMIX is written in the form CUSTOM IMIX - 123456...x, again with one letter per position in the sequence, but using capital letters. The tester must complete a table giving the letter for each size used, where each set of three lower-case letters is replaced by the integer size in octets. So aaa maps to A, bbb to B, ccc to C, ddd to D, eee to E, fff to F, ggg to G, and so on up to Z.

The example in the RFC is a five-packet sequence with sizes aaa = 64, aaa = 64, aaa = 64, ggg = 1020 and ggg = 1020, which is written CUSTOM IMIX - AAAGG. The custom form therefore carries two pieces of information: the order of the sizes, and the table that says what each letter means.
sections.plainLanguage: If the sizes you need are not standard, you name them yourself with capital letters and publish the list, so that the code and the list together describe the test exactly.

sections.title: Long or Random Sequences
sections.content:
When the genome cannot be used, because the sheer length of the sequence would make it unmanageable, five options are available. The first is run-length encoding, which may be specified when the sequence decomposes into a series of short repeating sequences: a table gives a count of repeating sequences and the packet-size sequence, for example a count of 20 for the sequence abcd, a count of 5 for ggga and a count of 10 for dcba. The same approach works for the custom form, with capital letters.

The second is a table of proportions, used when the sequence varies within proportional constraints. It gives the IP length, the percentage of the total and the length at other layers, for example 64 bytes at 23 per cent and 82 bytes at other layers, 128 bytes at 67 per cent and 146 bytes at other layers, and 1000 bytes at 10 per cent and 1018 bytes at other layers. This also allows non-standard packet sizes, but it trades the short genome specification and the ability to state the exact sequence for other flexibilities.

The third is a deterministic algorithm, such as a monotonic increase by one octet from a start value up to the maximum transmission unit, in which case the generation algorithm should be reported. The fourth is a pseudorandom length algorithm, where the algorithm should be reported along with the seed value; the RFC also recognises the opportunity to randomise the spacing between packets as well as the size, and says that both the spacing and length algorithms and seeds should be reported when used. The fifth is a pseudorandom sequence that generates an index into the table of packet lengths, where again the algorithm should be reported with the results, along with the seed value if one is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Very long or random sequences cannot be written out letter by letter. Instead you describe how they are made: how many times a short pattern repeats, what share of the traffic is each size, or the algorithm and seed that produce them.

sections.title: Keeping the Test Off the Production Network
sections.content:
Benchmarking as described in this memo is limited to technology characterisation using controlled stimuli in a laboratory environment, with dedicated address space and the other constraints of RFC 2544. The benchmarking network topology is an independent test setup and must not be connected to devices that may forward the test traffic into a production network or misroute traffic to the test management network.

Benchmarking is also performed on a black-box basis, relying solely on measurements observable from outside the device or system under test. Special capabilities should not exist in the device under test specifically for benchmarking purposes, and any implications for network security arising from the device should be identical in the lab and in production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The test lab has to stay separate from the real network, and the device under test must not get special treatment that would only exist for testing. What the test reveals about security should be true in the lab and in production alike.

items.label: MTU
items.desc: The maximum transmission unit; its length must be given in the report.

viz.caption: FIVE WAYS TO DESCRIBE A LONG OR RANDOM SEQUENCE

items.title: Run-length encoding
items.text: Give a count and a short pattern that repeats that many times.

items.title: Table of proportions
items.text: Give the share of the traffic at each size, plus the length at other layers.

items.title: Deterministic algorithm
items.text: Report the rule that generates the sizes, such as a step from a start value to the MTU.

items.title: Pseudorandom length
items.text: Report the algorithm and the seed value used to pick the lengths.

items.title: Pseudorandom sequence
items.text: Report the algorithm and seed that pick an index into the table of lengths.
